claim: Millions suffer from incurable lung diseases, and the donor lung shortage hampers organ transplants.
source: Millions suffer from incurable lung diseases, and the donor lung shortage hampers organ transplants.
evidence: This is a general statement about the clinical context, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Gastrulating Foxa2 lineage contributed to both lung mesenchyme and epithelium formation.
source: Using lineage-tracing mice and human pluripotent stem cell (PSC)-derived lung-directed differentiation, we revealed that gastrulating Foxa2 lineage contributed to both lung mesenchyme and epithelium formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage-tracing experiments in mice and human PSC differentiation studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Foxa2 lineage-derived cells in the lung mesenchyme progressively increased and occupied more than half of the mesenchyme niche, including endothelial cells, during lung development.
source: Interestingly, Foxa2 lineage-derived cells in the lung mesenchyme progressively increased and occupied more than half of the mesenchyme niche, including endothelial cells, during lung development.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative flow cytometry and immunostaining data showing progressive increase in Foxa2 lineage labeling during development.

claim: Foxa2 promoter-driven, conditional Fgfr2 gene depletion caused the lung and thymus agenesis phenotype in mice.
source: Foxa2 promoter-driven, conditional Fgfr2 gene depletion caused the lung and thymus agenesis phenotype in mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice showing lung and thymus agenesis.

claim: Wild-type donor mouse PSCs injected into blastocysts rescued the lung and thymus agenesis phenotype by complementing the Fgfr2-defective niche in the lung epithelium and mesenchyme and thymic epithelium.
source: Wild-type donor mouse PSCs injected into their blastocysts rescued this phenotype by complementing the Fgfr2-defective niche in the lung epithelium and mesenchyme and thymic epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by blastocyst complementation experiments showing rescue of the agenesis phenotype.

claim: Donor cells replaced the entire lung epithelial and robust mesenchymal niche during lung development, efficiently complementing the nearly entire lung niche.
source: Donor cell is shown to replace the entire lung epithelial and robust mesenchymal niche during lung development, efficiently complementing the nearly entire lung niche.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and immunostaining data showing high chimerism in complemented lungs.

claim: Rescued mice survived until adulthood with normal lung function.
source: Importantly, those mice survived until adulthood with normal lung function.
evidence: This is supported by respiratory function analysis and survival data of adult chimeric mice.

claim: The mammalian lung contains hundreds of airway branches and a thin micron-sized alveolar layer of inflated and well-vascularized alveoli composed of billions of cells from more than 50 different cell types.
source: It contains hundreds of airway branches and a thin micron-sized alveolar layer of inflated and well-vascularized alveoli composed of billions of cells from more than 50 different cell types (Crapo et al., 1982; Kotton and Morrisey, 2014; Stone et al., 1992; Travaglini et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing lung anatomy and cellular composition.

claim: Lung epithelial cells are derived from the foregut, definitive endoderm derivatives, classically labeled by Sox17 and Forkhead Box A2 (Foxa2).
source: The lung epithelial cells are derived from the foregut, definitive endoderm (DE) derivatives, classically labeled by Sox17 and Forkhead Box A2 (Foxa2) (Green et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies establishing the endodermal origin of lung epithelium.

claim: The entire Nkx2-1+ lung and tracheal epithelial primordium arises from Shh+ definitive endoderm.
source: Multiple genetic studies using Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) Cre lineage-tracing mice have also shown that the entire Nkx2-1+ lung and tracheal epithelial primordium arises from Shh+ DE (Cardoso and Kotton, 2008; Christodoulou et al., 2011; Harris et al., 2006; Kadzik and Morrisey, 2012; Tian et al., 2011; Weaver et al., 1999; Xing et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous lineage-tracing studies.

claim: The lung mesenchyme primordium is derived from Wnt2+ Isl1+ cardiopulmonary progenitors (CPP).
source: The lung mesenchyme primordium is derived from Wnt2+ Isl1+ cardiopulmonary progenitors (CPP) (Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study identifying CPP as the source of lung mesenchyme.

claim: CPP is the derivative of Osr1+ Nkx6-1+Barx1− Wnt4low foregut lung mesoderm that arises from lateral plate mesoderm (LPM).
source: CPP is the derivative of Osr1+ Nkx6-1+Barx1− Wnt4low foregut lung mesoderm that arises from lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) (Han et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study tracing the developmental origin of CPP.

claim: Mesendoderm is a bipotent transitional state between the primitive streak and nascent mesoderm labeled by Mixl1, Pdgfrα, and Brachyury (T) during gastrulation that can give rise to both definitive endoderm and mesoderm.
source: Mesendoderm is a bipotent transitional state between the PS and nascent mesoderm labeled by Mixl1, Pdgfrα, and Brachyury (T) during gastrulation that can give rise to both DE and mesoderm (Hart et al., 2002; Tada et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing mesendoderm.

claim: Pdgfrα is expressed in the epiblast-derived mesendoderm, the primitive endoderm (PrE), and its extra-embryonic endoderm derivatives, such as parietal and visceral endoderm, around E5.5–E7.5.
source: Pdgfrα is expressed in the epiblast-derived mesendoderm, the primitive endoderm (PrE), and its extra-embryonic endoderm derivatives, such as parietal and visceral endoderm, around E5.5–E7.5.
evidence: This is a statement about known expression patterns of Pdgfrα during early development.

claim: Foxa2 plays a pivotal role in alveolarization and airway goblet cell expansion.
source: Foxa2 plays a pivotal role in alveolarization and airway goblet cell expansion (Wan et al., 2004), while there was a significant knowledge gap regarding Foxa2 lineage during lung development.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on Foxa2 function.

claim: E12.5 morphometric analyses showed an extremely high proportion of lung mesenchyme labeling with tdTomato in PdgfraCreERT2/+; RosatdTomato/+ mice.
source: E12.5 morphometric analyses showed an extremely high proportion of lung mesenchyme labeling with tdTomato (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Among three embryos at E12.5, two showed 100% tdTomato labeling for lung mesenchyme markers, while one showed about 60% labeling in the mesenchyme.
source: Among three embryos at E12.5, two showed 100% tdTomato labeling for lung mesenchyme markers, while one showed about 60% labeling in the mesenchyme (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sma+ airway smooth muscle cells (86.9% ± 22.7), Pdgfrα+ lung mesenchyme (78.7% ± 36.9), and VE-cadherin+ endothelium (82.5% ± 30.4) were labeled with tdTomato in PdgfraCreERT2/+; RosatdTomato/+ mice at E12.5.
source: Sma+ airway smooth muscle cells (86.9% ± 22.7), Pdgfrα+ lung mesenchyme (78.7% ± 36.9), and VE-cadherin+ endothelium (82.5% ± 30.4) were labeled with tdTomato (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative morphometric data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Pdgfrα lineage labels 20.5% ± 18.3 of the lung epithelium.
source: In addition, the Pdgfrα lineage labels 20.5% ± 18.3 the lung epithelium (Figure 1B, arrows), suggesting that the contribution of the Pdgfrα lineage to the lung endoderm is limited.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from lineage-tracing experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 87.3% ± 5.26 of Mixl1+ cells within the primitive streak region expressed Pdgfrα protein.
source: We found that Mixl1+ within the PS region (Figure 1D, yellow dotted line), 87.3% ± 5.26 expressed Pdgfrα protein (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figures 1D, E, and F.

claim: Foxa2 lineage-driven tdTomato labeled 27.5% ± 1.15 of mid-streak primitive streak and 18.6% ± 8.93 in the Pdgfrα+ mesendoderm of primitive streak around mid-streak-stage embryos.
source: those Foxa2 lineage-driven tdTomato labeled 27.5% ± 1.15 of mid-streak PS and 18.6% ± 8.93 in the Pdgfrα+ mesendoderm of PS around mid-streak-stage embryos (Figure 1F, G, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from Foxa2 lineage-tracing experiments shown in Figures 1F and G.

claim: Foxa2-lineage labeled the entire lung epithelium and most of the lung mesenchyme at E16.5.
source: Using the Foxa2-lineage-tracing mice, we found from immunostaining that the Foxa2-lineage labeled the entire lung epithelium and most of the lung mesenchyme at E16.5 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: Foxa2-lineage labeled almost the entire lung epithelium (93.3% ± 2.00) and about 20% of lung mesenchyme (24.2% ± 5.51), including endothelial cells (16.8% ± 5.12) at E14.5.
source: Quantitative analyses by flow cytometry (FCM) in the E14.5 developing lungs of Foxa2-lineage-tracing mice showed that Foxa2-lineage labeled almost the entire lung epithelium (93.3% ± 2.00) and about 20% of lung mesenchyme (24.2% ± 5.51), including endothelial cells (16.8% ± 5.12) (Figure 2D, E)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: Foxa2-lineage-labeled cells increased dramatically throughout lung development.
source: Contrary to expectations, Foxa2-lineage-labeled cells increased dramatically throughout lung development (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data across developmental time points shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In adulthood, the Foxa2-lineage labeling reached about 99.97% ± 0.06 in lung epithelium, 51.3% ± 1.72 in lung mesenchyme, and 60.0% ± 8.44 in lung endothelial cells.
source: In adulthood, the Foxa2-lineage labeling reached about 99.97% ± 0.06 in lung epithelium, 51.3% ± 1.72 in lung mesenchyme, and 60.0% ± 8.44 in lung endothelial cells, with more than twofold change in the lung endothelium, compared with E14.5 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from adult mice shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Foxa2 lineage marked about 30–40% of E14.5 multiple cell types of lung mesenchyme such as Sma+ smooth muscle cells (31.9% ± 9.16), VE-cadherin+ (39.3% ± 12.5), or Pecam1+ (36.9% ± 10.4) endothelial cells, Pdgfrβ+ pericytes of the pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins (41.4% ± 10.5), and WT1+ mesothelial cells (31.9% ± 23.7).
source: Foxa2 lineage marked about 30–40% of E14.5 multiple cell types of lung mesenchyme such as Sma+ smooth muscle cells (31.9% ± 9.16), VE-cadherin+ (39.3% ± 12.5), or Pecam1+ (36.9% ± 10.4) endothelial cells, Pdgfrβ+ pericytes of the pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins (41.4% ± 10.5), and WT1+ mesothelial cells (31.9% ± 23.7) (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis data shown in Figures 2F and G.

claim: No clear Foxa2 protein level expression was observed in the mesenchyme of the embryonic lungs at E14.5 and E18.5.
source: Interestingly, no clear Foxa2 protein level expression was observed in the mesenchyme of the embryonic lungs at E14.5 and E18.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), consistent with previously reported Foxa2 protein expression patterns (Wan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citation to previous work.

claim: The LungMAP deposited single-cell RNA-seq database analysis showed a sporadic Foxa2 transcriptional expression pattern in developing lung mesenchyme, particularly in proliferating endothelium, on E15.5 and E17.5.
source: However, the LungMAP deposited single-cell RNA-seq database analysis showed a sporadic Foxa2 transcriptional expression pattern in developing lung mesenchyme, particularly in proliferating endothelium, on E15.5 and E17.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of publicly available single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Foxa2 transcriptional expression in lung mesenchyme was confirmed by in situ hybridization analysis on E18.5.
source: We confirmed Foxa2 transcriptional expression in lung mesenchyme by in situ hybridization analysis on E18.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: A slight increase in the relative expression of Foxa2 was observed in the tdTomato+ fraction of embryonic lung mesenchyme at E18.5.
source: We observed a slight increase in the relative expression of Foxa2 in the tdTomato+ fraction of embryonic lung mesenchyme, most likely contributing to the labeling in the Foxa2-lineage-tracing mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from sorted cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: tdTomato+ endothelial cells were found to have a slightly higher proliferative capacity than tdTomato− cells.
source: Furthermore, tdTomato+ endothelial cells were found to have a slightly higher proliferative capacity than tdTomato− cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: With the optimized protocol, various hiPSC lines efficiently induced a lung bud-like appearance, indicated by NKX2-1 expression in lung epithelial cells.
source: With this optimized protocol, various hiPSC lines efficiently induced a lung bud-like appearance, indicated by NKX2-1 expression in lung epithelial cells (Gotoh et al., 2014; Konishi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the differentiation protocol results and citations to previous work.

claim: On day 6, NKX2-1+ cells emerged in bud structure.
source: On day 6, NKX2-1+ cells emerged in bud structure (Figure 3B, asterisk, and S2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: On day 10, TBX4+ lung mesenchyme arose and surrounded the NKX2-1+SOX9+ lung epithelium.
source: On day 10, TBX4+ lung mesenchyme arose and surrounded the NKX2-1+SOX9+ lung epithelium (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 3B, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The budding morphology appeared 2.8% ± 0.90 per field on day 6 and progressively increased its proportion and reached around 57.4% ± 9.10.
source: The budding morphology appeared 2.8% ±0 .90 per field on day 6 and progressively increased its proportion and reached around 57.4% ± 9.10.
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis of the differentiation cultures.

claim: NKX2-1 was initially turned on 44.5% ± 6.41 at day 6, but the proportion progressively increased, and NKX2-1 was positive on the 95.9% ± 3.98 of day 15 budding structures.
source: Among the developing bud structures, NKX2-1 was initially turned on 44.5% ± 6.41 at day 6, but the proportion progressively increased, and NKX2-1 was positive on the 95.9% ± 3.98 of day 15 budding structures.
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis of NKX2-1 expression over time.

claim: SOX9 expression was found in 27.9% ± 13.1 of NKX2-1+ lung bud cells on day 8, but it dramatically increased and reached nearly 100% positive on day 15 (98.4% ± 1.98).
source: Interestingly, we found SOX9 expression in the 27.9% ± 13.1 of NKX2-1+ lung bud cells on day 8, but it dramatically increased and reached nearly 100% positive on day 15 (98.4% ± 1.98).
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis of SOX9 expression over time.

claim: NKX2-1 precedes the expression of SOX9.
source: This result indicated that NKX2-1 precedes the expression of SOX9.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression patterns of NKX2-1 and SOX9 during differentiation.

claim: The proportion of TBX4+ cells progressively increased in non-budding areas during the differentiation (48.2% ± 3.17).
source: The proportion of TBX4+ cells progressively increased in non-budding areas during the differentiation (48.2% ± 3.17).
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis of TBX4 expression.

claim: 12 hr after the Activin induction, more than 60% of the EPCAM+PDGFRα− primitive streak first turned on MIXL1, the mesendoderm marker.
source: Briefly, 12 hr after the Activin induction, more than 60% of the EPCAM+PDGFRα− PS first turned on MIXL1, the mesendoderm marker (Hart et al., 2002; Tada et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry kinetics data during differentiation and citations to previous work.

claim: After 36 hr, more than 90% of MIXL1+EPCAM+ mesoderm cells expressed PDGFRα.
source: After 36 hr, more than 90% of MIXL1+EPCAM+ mesoderm cells expressed PDGFRα.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry kinetics data during differentiation.

claim: Expression of FOXA2 appeared in some of those mesoderm cells at 36 hr.
source: At the same time, expression of FOXA2 appeared in some of those mesoderm cells (Figure 3E, F, asterisk).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: 72 hr later, mutual FOXA2 induction appeared when EPCAM+FOXA2+ definitive endoderm and EPCAM−FOXA2− lateral plate mesoderm were presented.
source: Thereafter, PDGFRα expression decreased, and 72 hr later, mutual FOXA2 induction appeared when EPCAM+FOXA2+ DE and EPCAM−FOXA2− LPM were presented (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: PDGFRα+ and FOXA2+ lineage are redundant but distinct stages of mesendoderm development.
source: These results suggest that PDGFRα+ and FOXA2+ lineage are redundant but distinct stages of mesendoderm development.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression patterns of PDGFRα and FOXA2 during differentiation.

claim: Mesendoderm is the lung precursor niche, with short-time window, contributing to both endodermal and mesodermal-derived lungs, evolutionally conserved across mouse development and human-directed differentiation.
source: It indicates that mesendoderm is the lung precursor niche, with short-time window, contributing to both endodermal and mesodermal-derived lungs, evolutionally conserved across mouse development and human-directed differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of mouse lineage tracing and human iPSC differentiation experiments.

claim: Systemic knockout mice of Fgf10 or Fgfr2 exhibit a phenotype of lung agenesis.
source: Mitotic signaling via Fgfr2 is required for both lung epithelium and mesenchyme, and systemic knockout mice of Fgf10 or Fgfr2 exhibit a phenotype of lung agenesis (Arman et al., 1999; De Langhe et al., 2006; De Moerlooze et al., 2000; Sekine et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Fgf10 and Fgfr2 knockout mice.

claim: Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice exhibited a lung agenesis phenotype and died at birth by respiratory distress.
source: We did not observe differences in the apparent gross morphology of embryos in Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice however, they exhibited a lung agenesis phenotype and died at birth by respiratory distress (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic analysis of Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice did not show agenesis phenotype in other major endodermal organs, such as the liver, esophagus, pancreas, and intestine.
source: We did not observe agenesis phenotype in other major endodermal organs, such as the liver, esophagus, pancreas, and intestine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kidney, glandular stomach, hair follicles, tooth bud, and limbs were preserved in Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice.
source: We also confirmed that kidney, glandular stomach, hair follicles, tooth bud, and limbs were preserved, which is known to form organ defective phenotype in the Fgfr2 systemic knockout (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Arman et al., 1999; De Langhe et al., 2006; De Moerlooze et al., 2000; Sekine et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: Thymus was found to be the agenesis phenotype in the Foxa2-driven Fgfr2 knockout mice.
source: while thymus was found to be the agenesis phenotype in the Foxa2-driven Fgfr2 knockout mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Donor nGFP+iPSCs generated whole lungs in Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice.
source: Strikingly, donor nGFP+iPSCs generated whole lungs in Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice, but general chimerism in other organs were diverse (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by blastocyst complementation experiments shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, and Table 1.

claim: Almost the entire lung epithelial, mesenchymal, and endothelial cell population at E17.5 was composed exclusively of nGFP+iPSCs in complemented Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice.
source: Importantly, almost the entire lung epithelial, mesenchymal, and endothelial cell population at E17.5 was composed exclusively of nGFP+iPSCs (Figure 4C–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and immunostaining data shown in Figures 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B-D.

claim: Wild-type, Shh-driven heterozygous, or knockout mice showed about 6.48–92.3% chimerism in the mesenchymal and endothelial lineages of the lung.
source: In contrast, wild-type, Shh-driven heterozygous, or knockout mice showed about 6.48–92.3% chimerism in the mesenchymal and endothelial lineages of the lung (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C, and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C, and Table 1.

claim: Sma+ lung airway mesenchyme (80.5 ± 12.0% vs 46.3 ± 16.6%, p = 0.0057), Pecam+ capillary (87.5 ± 7.5% vs 62.7 ± 15.9%, p = 0.0134), and NG2+ pericyte (80.6 ± 13.6% vs 57.5 ± 10.6%, p = 0.0171) showed higher chimerism in the complemented lungs of Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice than that of ShhCre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, Sma+ lung airway mesenchyme (80.5 ± 12.0% vs 46.3 ± 16.6%, p = 0.0057), Pecam+ capillary (87.5 ± 7.5% vs 62.7 ± 15.9%, p = 0.0134), and NG2+ pericyte (80.6 ± 13.6% vs 57.5 ± 10.6%, p = 0.0171) showed higher chimerism in the complemented lungs of Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 4) than that of ShhCre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis comparing Foxa2 and Shh-driven complementation shown in Figures 4F-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The rescued trachea of Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice exhibited higher chimerism in epithelium than that of ShhCre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice (95.4 ± 5.72% vs 70.82 ± 18.6%, p = 0.0223).
source: Given that the Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice showed shorter truncated trachea than ShhCre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A, B), the rescued trachea of Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice exhibited higher chimerism in epithelium than that of ShhCre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice (95.4 ± 5.72% vs 70.82 ± 18.6%, p = 0 .0223) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis of tracheal chimerism shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The PSC injection completely rescued both the thymus and lung aplasia phenotype, and lungs and thymus were co-generated in the Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice.
source: This result suggests that the PSC injection completely rescued both the thymus and lung aplasia phenotype, and lungs and thymus were co-generated in the Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by the rescue of both lung and thymus agenesis phenotypes in complemented mice.

claim: The chimerism in the Epcam+ thymic epithelium showed higher in Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice than ShhCre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice (92.4 ± 5.10% vs 28.7 ± 25.4%, p = 0.0006).
source: The chimerism in the Epcam+ thymic epithelium showed higher in Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice than ShhCre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice (92.4 ± 5.10% vs 28.7 ± 25.4%, p = 0 .0006) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry analysis of thymic epithelium shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fgfr2 is critical for lung epithelial cell development but also important for lung mesenchyme proliferation.
source: Previous reports described that Fgfr2 is critical for lung epithelial cell development but also important for lung mesenchyme proliferation (Yin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on Fgfr2 function.

claim: The percentage of Ki67+ proliferating cells was significantly higher in GFP+ donor cells compared to tdTomato+ host cells at E14.5.
source: Although tdTomato+ Fgfr2 knockout mesenchymal cells remained in early lung development at E14.5 (Figure 4I), the percentage of Ki67+ proliferating cells was significantly higher in GFP+ donor cells compared to tdTomato+ host cells (Figure 4J, K).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 proliferation analysis shown in Figures 4I-K.

claim: Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO, PSCCAG-GFP rescued mice survived at 4 weeks postnatal days without any difference in their gross appearance and behavior from the littermate control.
source: We found that Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO, PSCCAG-GFP rescued mice survived at 4 weeks postnatal days without any difference in their gross appearance and behavior from the littermate control; Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 hetero, PSCCAG-GFP mice (Figure 5A, asterisks).
evidence: This is supported by survival and phenotypic analysis of adult rescued mice shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Rescued mice showed no significant difference in their respiratory functions of f (frequency), TV (tidal volume), Raw (airway resistance), and EF50 (expiratory flow at the point 50% of TV is expired) compared to controls.
source: They showed no significant difference in their respiratory functions of f (frequency) (232.9 ± 18.5 vs 236.2 ± 25.7%, p = 0.790), TV (tidal volume) (0.253 ± 0.06 vs 0.233 ± 0.06, p = 0.514), Raw (airway resistance) (4.340 ± 1.65 vs 5.393 ± 3.80, p = 0.556), and EF50 (expiratory flow at the point 50% of TV is expired) (2.484 ±0 .513 vs 2.376 ±0 .860, p = 0.793) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by respiratory function analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FCM analyses confirmed a significantly lower proportion of the residual tdTomato+ host-derived cells in the epithelium (0.29% ± 0.40 vs 45.9% ± 24.1, p = 0.0004), mesenchyme (1.80% ± 1.94 vs 28.1% ± 11.5, p < 0.0001), and endothelium (3.86% ± 4.89 vs 44.6% ± 16.5, p < 0.0001) of the complemented adult lungs compared to the littermate control.
source: FCM analyses confirmed a significantly lower proportion of the residual tdTomato+ host-derived cells in the epithelium (0.29% ± 0.40 vs 45.9% ± 24.1, p = 0.0004), mesenchyme (1.80% ± 1.94 vs 28.1% ± 11.5, p < 0.0001), and endothelium (3.86% ± 4.89 vs 44.6% ± 16.5, p < 0.0001) of the complemented adult lungs compared to the littermate control (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry analysis of adult lungs shown in Figures 5E and F.

claim: PSCCAG-GFP injection into Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO blastocysts simultaneously rescued the thymus agenesis phenotype.
source: We also confirmed that PSCCAG-GFP injection into Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO blastocysts simultaneously rescued the thymus agenesis phenotype (Figure 5C, H, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by gross morphology and fluorescence imaging shown in Figures 5C and H.

claim: Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO provides defective niches in both lung epithelium and mesenchyme and thymic epithelium to be complemented by donor PSCs, enabling the entire lungs and thymus co-generation.
source: These results indicate that Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO provides defective niches in both lung epithelium and mesenchyme and thymic epithelium to be complemented by donor PSCs, enabling the entire lungs and thymus co-generation.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the combined results of complementation experiments.

claim: Donor cells formed about 50–80% chimerism in the complemented lung mesenchyme niches at E14.5.
source: Since donor cells formed about 50–80% chimerism in the complemented lung mesenchyme niches at E14.5 (Table 2) and endogenous Foxa2 lineage forms only 20–30% in the lung mesenchyme at E14.5, Fgfr2 defects at the Foxa2 lineage in early lung development are important but not sufficient for the complete lung mesenchyme niche complementation.
evidence: This is supported by chimerism data shown in Table 2.

claim: Losing Fgfr2 expression in Foxa2 lineage cells resulted in lower proliferative ability than donor cells during chimeric lung mesenchyme development.
source: Losing Fgfr2 expression in Foxa2 lineage cells resulted in lower proliferative ability than donor cells during chimeric lung mesenchyme development (Figure 4I–K), allowing progressive lung mesenchyme complementation in lung development and postnatal days, leading to promoting efficient whole lung generation.
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 proliferation analysis shown in Figures 4I-K.

claim: Targeting the endodermal lung lineage driven by Shh was sufficient for lung epithelial complementation but insufficient to generate whole lungs, and host-derived cells remained substantially in the mesodermal lung component.
source: Targeting the endodermal lung lineage driven by Shh was sufficient for lung epithelial complementation but insufficient to generate whole lungs, and host-derived cells remained substantially in the mesodermal lung component (Mori et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Gastrulating Pdgfrα lineage is the origin of the whole lung mesoderm, including endothelium.
source: In contrast to lung epithelial precursors, the orderly commitment and the origin of the entire pulmonary mesenchyme needed to be better defined. We showed that gastrulating Pdgfrα lineage is the origin of the whole lung mesoderm, including endothelium (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by Pdgfrα lineage-tracing data shown in Figures 1A and B.

claim: Foxa2 or Pdgfrα lineage labels a population primarily comprised of the earliest specified precursors in the distal compartment of mesendoderm.
source: Furthermore, Foxa2 or Pdgfrα lineage labels a population primarily comprised of the earliest specified precursors in the distal compartment of mesendoderm, similar to human iPSC cell-derived directed differentiation protocol.
evidence: This is supported by lineage-tracing data in mice and human iPSC differentiation experiments.

claim: PDGFRα+ mesendoderm primes the cell fate of Foxa2+ definitive endoderm after the MIXL1+ mesendoderm specification in the directed differentiation.
source: We uncovered that PDGFRα+ mesendoderm primes the cell fate of Foxa2+ DE after the MIXL1+ mesendoderm specification in the directed differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry kinetics data during human iPSC differentiation.

claim: The Foxa2 lineage+ mesenchyme did not show any discrete fates that would predict anatomical localization.
source: Intriguingly, the Foxa2 lineage+ mesenchyme did not show any discrete fates that would predict anatomical localization—depleting Fgfr2 in the Foxa2 lineage results in the loss of the Fgfr2 mitogen-mediated function of Foxa2 lineage+ lung mesenchyme, which leads to the loss of proliferative ability in most host lung mesenchyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Foxa2 lineage+ cells are distributed throughout the mesenchyme without specific localization.

claim: The combination of Fgfr2 depletion in Foxa2 lineage preserved other major organs, such as kidney, glandular stomach, hair follicles, tooth bud, and limbs, distinct from the agenesis or dysgenesis phenotype caused by the systemic Fgfr2 depletion.
source: We also found that the combination of Fgfr2 depletion in Foxa2 lineage preserved other major organs, such as kidney, glandular stomach, hair follicles, tooth bud, and limbs, distinct from the agenesis or dysgenesis phenotype caused by the systemic Fgfr2 depletion (Arman et al., 1999; De Langhe et al., 2006; De Moerlooze et al., 2000; Sekine et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and citations to previous work on systemic Fgfr2 knockout.

claim: The timing and the requirement of Fgfr2 are different from the lineage in each organ.
source: This is because the timing and the requirement of Fgfr2 are different from the lineage in each organ (Bates, 2011; Revest et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Fgfr2 function in different organs.

claim: Fgfr2 signaling is required for thymus formation, specifically in the Foxa2 lineage.
source: Our reports showed novel evidence of the requirement of Fgfr2 signaling for thymus formation, specifically in the Foxa2 lineage, associated with the previous statements regarding the critical role of Fgfr2 in thymus formation and thymic epithelial cell differentiation (Dooley et al., 2007; Revest et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the thymus agenesis phenotype in Foxa2Cre/+; Fgfr2 cKO mice and citations to previous work.

claim: Thymus formation is essentially formed in the Foxa2 lineage but not Shh.
source: This study showed evidence that thymus formation is essentially formed in the Foxa2 lineage but not Shh, supported by the previous report that the dynamic Shh expression regulates larynx-esophageal separation and esophageal constriction on the fourth pharyngeal pouches above the lungs during development (Ramachandran et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by the differential thymus phenotypes in Foxa2 vs Shh-driven Fgfr2 knockout mice and citation to previous work.

claim: In complemented mice with rescued thymus, immune cells were most likely educated in self-recognition by donor cells' derived thymus epithelium and induced central tolerance.
source: In these complemented mice, immune cells were most likely educated in self-recognition by donor cells' derived thymus epithelium and induced central tolerance.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of thymus in immune cell education and the high chimerism of donor cells in thymic epithelium.

claim: GvHD is a crucial risk factor for long-term survival following human lung transplantation.
source: It is also important to note that GvHD is a crucial risk factor for long-term survival following human lung transplantation (Bos et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on lung transplantation outcomes.
